lines.text: This is the Functional Analysis Screening Tool, the FAST. It is a sixteen-item yes-or-no questionnaire that a teacher, a parent, or anyone who knows the student well answers about one problem behavior. It was published by Iwata, DeLeon, and Roscoe in 2013, and this sheet is the workstation's scoring worksheet for it.

The sixteen items fall into four groups of four. Items one to four ask about social positive reinforcement: attention, or getting preferred items. Items five to eight ask about social negative reinforcement: escape from tasks and demands. Items nine to twelve ask about automatic reinforcement, sensory stimulation, and thirteen to sixteen about automatic reinforcement that eases pain or discomfort.

Before anyone answers, settle the target behavior. Write one behavior and its operational definition on the Setup sheet, and read the same definition to every informant. The FAST is scored one behavior at a time, so a second target gets its own administration.

Then choose the informants: people who see the behavior often, in the routines where it happens. Record each one here, with their role, how long they have known the student, and how much time they spend in those routines. Each informant answers on their own, without conferring, within a few days of the others, and it takes about fifteen to twenty minutes.
Enter each informant's answers by item number: Y for yes, N for no. Informant A goes in the first column, informant B in the second. The sheet counts as you type.
N A means the informant has not seen that situation and cannot say. An item that either informant answered N A is left out of that pair's agreement, as the original analysis did.

The totals table counts the yes answers in each group, for each informant. The outcome is the group with the most yes answers; the published FAST has no margin rule. The sheet shades each informant's highest total.

The verdict reads the totals out. When the highest group leads the next by a single item, the sheet keeps the outcome and adds a caution: a one-item margin was typical of the FAST outcomes that matched the functional analysis in the study, so it is not weak, but it is not much. When two groups tie, there is no outcome.

With two or more informants, the Agree column shows how often the pairs answered an item the same way, and the verdict gives each pair's item agreement. In the study, across 196 pairs of informants, the mean item agreement was 71.5 percent. The pairs ranged from 28.6 to 100 percent, and most fell between 61 and 80. Against the 80 percent held to for direct observation, the authors called the reliability moderate at best.

The last figure compares each item with the published sample. Agreement ran from 53.3 percent on item twelve to 84.5 percent on item four, and the items about what happens before the behavior agreed more often, 78.9 percent, than the items about what happens after, 67.7. An item your informants disagree on, or one that sits well below the published value, is one to ask about in the follow-up interview.

Agreement on the outcome itself, the group each informant's answers point to, was 64.8 percent. So about one pair in three pointed to different functions for the same behavior. That is why the FAST goes to more than one informant, and why their disagreement is information, not noise.

How well does the outcome predict a functional analysis? In the second study, 69 problem behaviors were screened with the FAST and then tested with a functional analysis. The FAST outcome matched the analysis 63.8 percent of the time: 77.8 percent for social positive reinforcement, 56 percent for social negative, and 61.5 percent for automatic.

When the two informants agreed on the outcome, the match rose to 70.8 percent, and for social positive reinforcement it was seven of seven. When informants point the same way, the FAST is at its most useful. When they split, it is telling you to look further.

So what do the results help determine? The FAST is a screening tool. The authors wrote that it gives the interview a consistent format and helps design the functional analysis; it does not replace one, and on its own it is not an adequate basis for treatment.

Section one of the FAST is open-ended: when and where the behavior is most and least likely, who is present, and what usually happens before and after. Summarize it here and compare it with the item answers. An informant who answered no to the escape items but wrote that the behavior starts when worksheets are handed out has given you a clarifying question, and something to observe.

Then decide the next step. Strong concurrence across informants and instruments can justify testing that one function first. Disagreement calls for the interview, observation, and a full analysis. Endorsed pain items route to a medical screen before anything else. And after the functional analysis, record its outcome on the Convergence sheet, so the practice keeps its own record of how often the FAST was right.
Screen. Ask. Then test.
Your turn. Pause here, read the last informant's totals on the card, and decide: which group is the outcome, and by how much? Then play on.
The outcome is the group with the most yes answers, and the margin is the gap to the next group. A margin of one is kept, with a caution. A tie is no outcome.

This short guide is for you, the person answering the FAST, the Functional Analysis Screening Tool. It asks sixteen yes-or-no questions about one behavior, and it takes about fifteen to twenty minutes.
Answer about the one behavior named at the top, as it was defined for you, and nothing else. If two behaviors come to mind, ask which one is meant before you start.
For each question, choose yes if what it describes is usually true for this behavior, and no if it is not. Go with what you have actually seen, not what you would guess.
If you have never been in that situation with the student, choose N A, not applicable. That is a better answer than a guess, and it is left out of the scoring.

Answer on your own, without talking it over with anyone else first. The assessor compares the answers afterwards, and the differences are useful. Then write a few words in the open-ended section: when and where the behavior happens most, and what usually comes before and after it.
One behavior. Your own answers. Yes, no, or not seen.

This is the Convergence sheet, where every indirect result meets. Each row is one informant's highest category on one instrument, mapped to a common set: attention, tangible, escape, automatic, and physical.
A FAST social-positive outcome counts as attention or tangible, because the FAST does not separate them. A row flagged weak, a tie or nothing endorsed, is shown but not counted.

Consensus is counted by informant, not by row, so one person who answered five instruments does not outvote the others. Each informant's vote is their most frequent category across what they completed.

The verdict names the leading category and its share of the informants. This form asks for at least three informants with an outcome, and treats eighty percent or more as agreement. A majority without agreement is a hypothesis to test, not a conclusion.
Wherever a physical or pain profile leads, the sheet says so first: a medical or nursing referral comes before any behavioral conclusion.

The figure shows the same thing two ways: the informants behind each category, and the counted outcomes. They are counted, not averaged, because averaging mixes reliable and unreliable answers to an unknown degree.

The hypothesis statement is drafted from the sheet into the empty fields: setting events, the antecedent, the behavior, the consequence, the competing hypothesis to rule out, and the idiosyncratic variables the interviews named. It is a draft. Edit it.

Then the decision: descriptive assessment in the routines the informants named, a medical referral first, a full analysis, a single-function test when agreement is strong on attention or tangible, or a follow-up interview on the items the informants disagreed on.

After the functional analysis, enter its outcome, the date and the design. The sheet scores each instrument's correspondence, one, a half, or zero per pair, as Iwata and colleagues did, and sets it beside the published rates, so the practice keeps its own validity record.
Converge. Decide. Verify.
